summary: Saugerties' 1869 brick lighthouse on a Hudson River granite crib; keeper Katie Crowley made rescues in the 1870s. Now a conservancy museum and bed-and-breakfast.

lens.where: Museum on the second floor of the lighthouse (LighthouseFriends); the Coast Guard exchanged a fourth-order lens on display for the sixth-order lens the light used

access.note: Grounds open; the dwelling and tower open for tours on summer Sundays (June through August) and to overnight guests. The walk is a half-mile trail through the Ruth Reynolds Glunt Nature Preserve, which floods at high tide.

stay.note: Overnight rooms run by the Saugerties Lighthouse Conservancy

events.note: Congress appropriates $5,000 (June 30, 1834) for a lighthouse at the mouth of Esopus Creek
Light begins operation with Abraham Persons as first keeper (LighthouseFriends and the roster; the Digital Archive gives 1836 as the year established)
Fire destroys the original lighthouse
Second lighthouse rebuilt on the old site by 1850
Sixth-order Fresnel lens replaces the lamps and reflectors
Congress appropriates $25,000 (March 2, 1867) for a replacement lighthouse
Brick tower on a circular granite crib; keeper's quarters the same year (Italianate brick)
Old wooden lighthouse replaced and sold
Katie Crowley made official keeper
Katie Crowley reaches a young couple who fell through the ice; she pulls the woman from under the ice and she regains consciousness (LighthouseFriends only)

Sloop loaded with bluestone overturns near the lighthouse in a storm; Katie and Ellen Crowley launch the station boat. Year is approximate: LighthouseFriends prints a captain's account published in 1878 but does not date the rescue
Harbor enlarged by jetties; road built along the north jetty to the lighthouse
Boathouse moved from the rear to the front of the pier; fence and gates built (Board entry 414)
Wooden platform added to the top of the tower to hold a fog bell
Keeper Conrad Hawk receives the efficiency flag for calendar year 1920
Keeper Conrad Hawk dies January 8, 1940, after 26 years (LighthouseFriends)
Keeper told in February 1954 the light would be automated in spring; tender's crew strips the house
Discontinued 1954 (Digital Archive gives 1954-1990 as the discontinued period)
Coast Guard plans to demolish the vandalized lighthouse; Ruth Reynolds Glunt campaigns to save it (LighthouseFriends: 'a decade later'; year approximate)
Placed on the National Register of Historic Places (LighthouseFriends, 1978; the NRHP date could not be checked in the record read)
Saugerties Lighthouse Conservancy established
Conservancy purchases the lighthouse and surrounding wetlands for $1
Solar-powered light installed by the Coast Guard is activated August 4, 1990

corrections.why: The light was first lit in 1835 or 1836 (see resolved_conflicts). The 1990 event is the Coast Guard's solar light being activated in the restored lighthouse, a relight, not the first light.
The Digital Archive gives 40.5 feet above mean high water (12.3 m). No source we read gives 8.5 m.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: LighthouseFriends says the light commenced operation in 1835 with Abraham Persons as first keeper, and the Digital Archive roster begins with Persons in 1835. The Digital Archive's place record gives 1836 as the year established, and the record's source (Rowlett) also gives 1836. The first light is most likely 1835, and 1836 may be the year the station was formally established. Not fully resolved.

LighthouseFriends gives 1978 for the National Register listing. The Digital Archive page read gives no listing date, and the nomination PDF (NRHP 79001642) is a 'not yet digitized' placeholder in our copy, so the date cannot be checked here. The story gives only the LighthouseFriends date.

The conservancy's home page offers tours of the interior and tower on summer Sundays, June through August. LighthouseFriends gives Sundays from Memorial Day through Labor Day, noon to 3 p.m., or by appointment. The story gives both; check before visiting.

notes_for_editor: The NRHP nomination PDF for 79001642 is the 'not yet digitized' placeholder, so no nomination text was read. The 1875 and 1878 rescues rest on LighthouseFriends alone; the 1878 account is LighthouseFriends' quotation of a captain's account, which it cites to The Chatham Courier of 25 December 1878 ('A Pair of Ida Lewises'). We did not read the newspaper. Chronicling America returned HTTP 520 for every search tried (a search for 'Katie Crowley' and Saugerties, 1873-1885, failed), so no newspaper material is used. The record's characteristic 'Fl G 4s', range 4.0 nm and tower height 14.0 m are not supported by any source we read. Wikipedia (not cited) gives Oc W 4s, 13 m focal height, 5 nm range, and a 1838 earlier lighthouse; a Light List check is needed (record LLNR 1-38375). Katie Crowley's and Dorcas Schoonmaker's roles are as the roster gives them, 'principal keeper'. Dorcas Schoonmaker appears in the roster and in LighthouseFriends' head-keeper list; no sex or other detail is given for her, so the story does not describe her. The 1899 Board entry's printed page is not confirmed (scan page 110). The keepers' roster is the Digital Archive's (NARA registers via the Kraig Anderson inventory); no keeper was checked against a primary register here. Children injured in the 1916 battery accident are not named. LighthouseFriends' description of Pastorini's feelings on leaving is omitted; only the automation notice is used. Fact-check 2026-10-22: removed the claim that the roster gives two women keepers (only Katie Crowley is a woman in the sources read); removed the '1979' NRHP date, which the Digital Archive page read does not show; the 1899 boathouse move is the Board's entry 414, and the earlier move is LighthouseFriends' account. Hawk's flag citation is the Bulletin 1921 list on PDF p. 14 (the flag announcement is on PDF p. 13).
